Chapter 4: The Difference Between Teaching Religion and Teaching About Religion
One of the biggest challenges to boosting religious literacy in the United States is this ongoing confusion: what does it really mean to teach about religion in public settings, especially in our schools? If you’ve ever worried that having any conversation about religion in the classroom might cross a line—maybe even threaten the separation of church and state—you’re definitely not alone. This fear has led a lot of people to avoid the topic altogether, which means students often miss out on learning about a huge part of our world’s history and culture.
But here’s where things get interesting: there’s a big difference between teaching religion and teaching about religion. When someone is teaching religion, they’re encouraging students to embrace certain beliefs or practices—to actually adopt a particular faith. That’s not what public schools are about. Public education is built around neutrality, and respecting the many different backgrounds students bring with them.
Teaching about religion, though, is a whole different story. It means giving students the facts—sharing the beliefs, the histories, and the rituals of different traditions—without pushing them to accept any one of them. Think about it like this: in civics class, you learn about democracy, monarchy, and other political systems, but nobody’s telling you which one to believe in. Or in literature, you might read the Bible as literature, right alongside Shakespeare or the Odyssey, but you’re not being asked to take it on faith.
The real goal here is understanding, not conversion.
So, how does teaching about religion actually show up in the classroom? It could mean exploring the stories and symbols that ground different traditions, or diving into the historical moments that shaped major religious movements. Maybe it’s tracing how faith has inspired art, music, and even politics. Ultimately, we want students to have the tools to make sense of the world around them, join in meaningful conversations, and appreciate just how diverse human experience can be.
There are a few essential principles to keep in mind for teaching about religion in a way that’s fair and respectful:
First, neutrality—teachers shouldn’t promote or put down any religion. The information has to be balanced and objective.
Next, inclusivity—it’s important to cover a wide range of religious traditions, even those that aren’t as well-known or have been marginalized in the past.
Then, there’s critical thinking. Students should feel comfortable asking questions, analyzing sources, and really thinking through the role of religion in society.
And finally, respect for diversity. Every student deserves to feel respected and included, no matter their background.
Of course, putting these principles into practice isn’t always simple. It takes thoughtful planning, solid teacher training, and support from both administrators and families. And maybe most of all, it calls for open, honest conversations—admitting that religion has the power both to unite and to divide.
But when we make this distinction clear, it really opens the door to a public education system where learning about religion is viewed as a key part of becoming an informed citizen, not a threat to neutrality. In the end, this approach helps students—and all of us—navigate a complex world, strengthening democracy by encouraging deeper, more thoughtful engagement with the religious threads woven through public life.
